content:
An advocate or law firm in India can have a website, but it is not a marketing website in the usual sense. Rule 36 of the Bar Council of India Rules forbids advocates from soliciting work or advertising, directly or indirectly. A 2008 amendment, made after a Supreme Court direction, allows advocates to publish a limited set of factual particulars on a website: who they are, how to reach them, where they are enrolled and, depending on the reading of the Schedule, their qualifications and areas of practice. So the job of a website designer in Pune building a site for a lawyer is unusual. The goal is not to persuade a stranger to hire you. It is to give a person who already has your name, or who was referred to you, an accurate, professional, easy-to-use record, and to avoid every feature that would turn that record into an advertisement.

This guide is written for advocates, partners in small and mid-sized law firms, and office managers in Pune and elsewhere in Maharashtra who are commissioning or rebuilding a firm website. It explains what the rule says, what the 2024 Madras High Court judgment and the Bar Council's follow-up changed in practice, which pages and features are generally safe, which are risky, and how to brief a developer so the build does not create a disciplinary problem. It is not legal advice. The Bar Council's own published rules and your State Bar Council are the authorities; where this article says "check", it means check with them.

## What Rule 36 actually restricts

Rule 36 sits in Part VI, Chapter II of the Bar Council of India Rules, among the standards of professional conduct. In plain terms it says an advocate shall not solicit work or advertise, whether by circulars, advertisements, touts, personal communications, interviews not warranted by personal relations, newspaper comments or photographs produced in connection with cases they have been engaged in. It also says the advocate's sign-board or name-plate should be of reasonable size and should not suggest that the advocate is or has been a judge, an Advocate-General or similar.

The rule exists because the profession treats legal services as something other than commerce. The Madras High Court put it bluntly in its July 2024 judgment: the legal profession is not a business.

### The 2008 website proviso

In 2008, following a direction from the Supreme Court, the Bar Council amended Rule 36 to add a proviso allowing advocates to furnish information on their websites. The commonly cited particulars in the Schedule are:

- name;
- address, telephone numbers and email;
- enrolment number, date of enrolment, and the State Bar Council where the advocate was originally enrolled and is currently registered;
- professional and academic qualifications;
- areas of practice.

The proviso also requires that the information be furnished "under intimation to and as approved by" the Bar Council of India, and secondary sources describe a declaration that the information is accurate. Commentators do not all quote the list identically, so before you sign off your content, read the current text of the rules on the Bar Council of India website and, if in doubt, ask your State Bar Council what intimation it expects.

The practical reading most firms adopt: **facts about you are allowed; claims designed to attract work are not.**

## What changed in 2024

For years, many advocates treated the website proviso loosely, and lawyer-listing platforms flourished. That changed in July 2024.

On 3 July 2024 the Madras High Court, in a public interest petition (P.N. Vignesh v. the Chairman and Members of the Bar Council of India), held that online platforms such as Quikr, Sulekha and Justdial that offered lawyer services were in effect selling legal services and soliciting work, contrary to Rule 36. The court said these platforms could not shelter behind the intermediary protection in Section 79 of the Information Technology Act for activity that is illegal under the Advocates Act and the Bar Council Rules. It directed the Bar Council to act against advocates who advertise and against the platforms, and directed the platforms to remove violating content.

Within days, on 8 July 2024, the Bar Council of India issued a press release and a circular asking all State Bar Councils to take disciplinary action against advocates advertising or soliciting work through online portals, and sent cease-and-desist notices to several platforms. Sulekha challenged the judgment in the Supreme Court, arguing among other things that the 2008 amendment permits the listed details to be published online; the Supreme Court issued notice to the Bar Council. At the time of writing we have not found a final Supreme Court ruling on that petition, so treat the High Court position as the operative caution. TODO: check the status of the Sulekha special leave petition before each annual review of this article.

What this means for your own website: the judgment was about third-party listing and lead-selling platforms, not about an advocate's own factual website. But it signals how strictly the profession reads "solicit" and "advertise" today. A firm site that behaves like a lead-generation funnel — paid ads pointing to it, "Get a free consultation in 10 minutes" banners, client-win counters — invites exactly the complaint the Bar Councils have been told to act on.

## The pages a compliant law firm website usually has

Here is the structure we would propose for a small firm or an independent practice. Every page sticks to verifiable facts.

### 1. The entry disclaimer

Most Indian law firm websites open with a disclaimer that the visitor must accept before seeing content. A typical wording says that the Bar Council of India does not permit advocates to solicit work or advertise, that by clicking "I agree" the visitor acknowledges they are seeking information of their own accord and that there has been no solicitation, and that nothing on the site is legal advice or creates a lawyer-client relationship.

Build notes:

- **Make it a real, accessible dialog.** It must be keyboard-operable, readable by screen readers, and the "I agree" button must be a proper button element. A disclaimer that traps keyboard users is a poor first impression for a firm.
- **Remember the choice** for the session (or for a sensible period) so a visitor is not asked on every page.
- **Do not hide your content from Google behind it.** Render the page content in the HTML and overlay the disclaimer on top, rather than loading content only after a click. Google can then read the page. Google's guidance on intrusive interstitials specifically lists legally required dialogs as an acceptable case, so a legally motivated overlay is not the problem it would be on a shop.
- **Put the same text on a permanent Disclaimer page** linked from the footer, so it is readable at any time.

### 2. Home page

A short factual statement: the name of the firm or advocate, the city and courts where you practise (for example, the District and Sessions Court in Pune, the Bombay High Court, tribunals), the main areas of practice, and contact details. No slogans like "Pune's most trusted lawyers" or "We win". A clean typographic layout with a good photograph of the office or the advocates does more for credibility than a stock image of a gavel.

### 3. Advocates / People

One profile per advocate, each containing the particulars the Schedule contemplates:

- full name and designation within the firm (Partner, Associate, Of Counsel);
- enrolment number, date of enrolment and the State Bar Council;
- degrees and the institutions that awarded them;
- areas of practice;
- languages spoken (factual and useful to clients in Pune, where many prefer Marathi or Hindi);
- a professional email.

Things to leave out or think hard about: lists of named clients, "successful outcomes", rankings bought from directories, and photographs taken at court with matter details visible. Publications and teaching positions are commonly included by firms as factual professional information; whether they cross the line is a judgement call you should take yourself, ideally with your Bar Council's view in hand.

### 4. Areas of practice

A page (or one page per area) that describes in neutral language what the area covers: "Property and real estate: title verification, documentation for sale and lease, registration, and disputes before civil courts and RERA". This is factual information about your practice.

What turns a practice page into advertising is outcome language and urgency: "We get your bail in 24 hours", "100% success rate in divorce cases", "Lowest fees in Pune". Leave those out. If you are writing for search, write educational content in a separate, clearly labelled section (see below), not sales copy on the practice page.

### 5. Contact

Address with a map embed, office hours, phone, email, and directions to the office (parking near Shivajinagar court traffic is genuinely useful information). A contact form is fine if it is a means of contacting the office rather than a funnel. Keep it short: name, phone or email, a general subject, and a free-text box, with a clear note not to send confidential details or documents through the form until an engagement is agreed. That note matters: a stranger may paste the whole facts of a dispute into a form, and you do not want unsolicited confidential information sitting in a web host's mailbox.

### 6. Disclaimer, privacy and terms

Alongside the disclaimer, publish a privacy notice describing what the contact form collects, where it goes, who sees it and how long it is kept. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the DPDP Rules notified in November 2025 make a clear notice good practice for anyone collecting personal data through a website; have the notice reviewed by your own colleagues, who will know the law better than any web agency.

## Features that are risky or should be left out

These are the features we decline or advise against when building for advocates, because each can read as solicitation:

- **Client testimonials and star ratings.** A testimonial is an endorsement used to attract new clients. Even if a client volunteers one, publishing it on your site is hard to reconcile with Rule 36. This is the reverse of our advice for most service businesses, where we recommend honest, permission-based testimonials (see our guide to [showing testimonials and reviews on a service website](/blog/website-designer-pune-testimonials-reviews-section-review-schema-2026/)).
- **Case results and "wins".** Publishing outcomes, especially with party names, both advertises and can breach client confidentiality.
- **Live chat widgets that pop up with "Need a lawyer? Chat now".** A visitor-initiated contact option is one thing; a proactive invitation to engage is another.
- **WhatsApp pop-ups and floating "Consult now" bars.** A plain WhatsApp number among contact details is a contact detail. A flashing sticky button with sales copy is a call to action.
- **Fee offers, discounts and "free first consultation" banners.**
- **Paid search and social ads pointing to the site.** This is a marketing decision, not a design one, but it is the most direct form of advertising. Discuss it with your Bar Council before spending anything.
- **Lead-generation landing pages** for terms like "divorce lawyer in Pune" built to capture enquiries. Even if technically a page on your own domain, this is the funnel model the Madras judgment criticised.
- **Third-party listing and "consult a lawyer" platforms.** This is outside the website itself, but your website should not link to your profiles on them as though they were endorsements.

## Content and search: what is reasonable

People do search for lawyers, and a law firm website that Google cannot understand helps nobody, including clients who already have your name and are trying to find your number. A few things are both reasonable and useful:

- **Accurate business information.** A correctly marked-up name, address and phone number, consistent with your Google Business Profile, helps people who search for your firm by name. Our guide to [LocalBusiness schema](/blog/web-development-company-pune-localbusiness-schema-nap-opening-hours-2026/) covers the mechanics; for a law firm, the `LegalService` type (a subtype of LocalBusiness on schema.org) or `Attorney` can be used, but do not add review or rating markup.
- **Educational articles.** Explaining a change in law, a new procedure or a common question in neutral, informative language is what many firms do under a "Publications", "Insights" or "Updates" heading. Keep it informative, date every article, avoid "call us now" endings, and include a short note that the article is general information and not legal advice. Whether a given article crosses into solicitation depends on its tone; when in doubt, cut the sales language.
- **Fast, accessible pages.** A slow site with a broken disclaimer modal reflects badly on the firm whether or not anyone is marketing.

Avoid buying links, joining "top lawyers in Pune" listicles that charge for inclusion, and keyword-stuffed location pages ("best criminal lawyer in Kothrud, Baner, Aundh..."). These are poor practice for any website and, for advocates, they look like advertising.

## A worked example: a three-advocate practice in Pune

Consider a hypothetical practice of three advocates working mainly in property, family and consumer matters before the Pune courts and the consumer commission, with one office in Sadashiv Peth. A sensible site for them would have:

1. Entry disclaimer overlay, plus a permanent Disclaimer page.
2. Home: firm name, "Advocates practising in Pune since [year]" (only if the year is accurate), courts and forums, three practice areas, office address and phone.
3. Advocates: three profiles with enrolment details, qualifications, languages and areas of practice, each with a professional photograph taken in the office.
4. Practice areas: three neutral descriptions.
5. Updates: four or five plain-language notes on recent changes relevant to property and consumer matters, each dated.
6. Contact: map, hours, phone, email and a short form with the confidentiality note.
7. Privacy notice and terms.

That is eight to twelve pages. It is a modest site, and that modesty is the point.

## What it typically costs and how long it takes

For a factual firm website of this kind, built on WordPress or as a lightweight custom site, with a professional design, the disclaimer dialog, advocate profiles, a contact form, basic schema and a privacy notice, budgets in Pune typically fall in these indicative ranges:

- **Independent advocate or two-person practice (6–10 pages):** roughly ₹30,000 to ₹70,000.
- **Small to mid-sized firm (10–25 pages, multiple advocate profiles, an updates section, Marathi and English):** roughly ₹70,000 to ₹2,00,000.
- **Larger firms with a publications library, multiple offices, intranet or client document portal:** a custom quote, often well above that.

These are indicative ranges, not a quotation; the drivers are the number of profiles, languages, whether you need a client portal, and how much writing you need help with. Timelines are usually three to six weeks, and the slowest part is nearly always the content: getting each advocate's particulars, photographs and practice-area text approved by the partners.

Ongoing costs are hosting, domain, SSL renewal and maintenance (updates and backups), which for a small site are usually a few thousand rupees a year to a few thousand a month depending on the level of care.

## How to brief your website designer

Give your developer this list at the start and you will save weeks of rework:

1. **Compliance first.** Tell them the site must follow Rule 36 and that you will approve every line of text. A designer who has only built for shops and clinics will default to testimonials, sticky call buttons and "book now" language.
2. **The particulars for each advocate,** in the exact form you want published.
3. **Your disclaimer, privacy notice and terms text,** drafted or approved by the firm.
4. **Languages.** If you want Marathi and English, say so up front; it affects structure, fonts and URL design.
5. **Contact routing.** Who receives form submissions, and should they also be stored in a simple database or a CRM so nothing is lost when someone is in court all day?
6. **No tracking surprises.** Decide whether you want analytics at all. If you do, keep it to privacy-respecting measurement and disclose it in the privacy notice; do not let a designer add marketing pixels by default.
7. **Ownership.** The domain, hosting account and source should be in the firm's name, not the developer's. Put ownership, escrow and warranty terms in the contract in writing.

## The parallel with other regulated professions

Law is not the only profession where a website has to inform without soliciting. Doctors face the National Medical Commission's rules, and we have written separately about [designing a clinic or doctor website under the NMC advertising guidelines](/blog/website-designer-pune-clinic-doctor-website-nmc-advertising-guidelines-2026/). Chartered accountants have their own ICAI guidelines on websites. The design pattern is similar across all three: factual pages, careful profiles, no testimonials or outcome claims, and contact routes that are available rather than pushed.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can lawyers in India have a website?

Yes. Since the 2008 amendment to Rule 36 of the Bar Council of India Rules, advocates may publish certain factual particulars on a website, such as name, contact details, enrolment details, qualifications and areas of practice. The website must inform, not solicit work or advertise, and the information is to be furnished under intimation to the Bar Council.

### Why do law firm websites in India show a disclaimer before you enter?

Because the Bar Council of India does not permit advocates to solicit work or advertise. The entry disclaimer records that the visitor is seeking information on their own initiative, that there has been no solicitation, and that the site is not legal advice. It should be an accessible dialog and the content behind it should still be readable by search engines.

### Can an advocate put client testimonials or case results on their website?

It is best avoided. Testimonials, ratings and published case wins are used to attract new clients and are hard to reconcile with Rule 36. Case results can also expose client information. Most firms leave them out entirely.

### Can advocates list themselves on Justdial, Sulekha or similar platforms?

In July 2024 the Madras High Court held that such platforms offering lawyer services violated Rule 36, and the Bar Council of India asked State Bar Councils to act against advocates soliciting work through online portals. Sulekha has challenged the judgment in the Supreme Court. Until that is decided, treat paid listings and lead platforms as a serious disciplinary risk and take advice from your Bar Council.

### How much does a law firm website cost in Pune?

For a factual site with an entry disclaimer, advocate profiles, practice areas and a contact page, indicative budgets run from about ₹30,000 to ₹70,000 for an individual practice and ₹70,000 to ₹2,00,000 for a small or mid-sized firm, depending on the number of profiles, languages and any client portal.
